blocks.x: The End This is an interview with Mr. Singh Miller. This is Bill Russell doing the interviewing. And the date is about the tenth of... Is this the eleventh? Lost track of the date. The eleventh of December, 1964. We're recording this down at 732 St. Peter Street. What is your full name? My name is James Edward Miller. James Edward Miller. Everyone calls me Singh. How did you get that nickname? I've been singing since I was a little bit of a boy. Actually, from your singing? From school days. Now, where were you born? Born in New Orleans. Right here in New Orleans. What part of town? I was born in the Twelfth Ward. In the Twelfth Ward. Let's see, is that the... On Gentile Street, Gentile Annunciation. Downtown then? Uptown. Oh, Annunciation. My daddy was a musician. My daddy used to be a piccolo player. I used to listen to him play all the time when I was a boy. And I said, I hope that when I grow up I'll learn how to play some type of music. But when I started playing music, I had a violin like you did, but I made a ukulele out of my violin. Oh, and I just picked it then. And started picking it. So I started up with some boys, four fellas, they're still living. Eddie Hickman, Julius Simpson, and a saxophone player, he's dead now. Can't call his name no more now. Did you get the date when you were born? June 17, 1913. 1913. And about how old were you then when you first played in that time? Well, I first started music. I started around 1920. My first job playing I was around 1927. Playing music around 1927. I played at the O.K. Lounge. We used to play two nights a week, Friday and Saturday, Cutler's Giant. What was that about? On Tulane? No, it was on the South Street. Oh, on the South. On the South Street. Then I started going from joint to joint. I met Kit Howard. I got in his band. I started playing with him. I played with Henry Russ. He brought me a long ways. Father Al helped me a long ways. I played the banjo for a while. I used to go try to play the banjo. And Father Al, in his place. I still could play the banjo, still have my banjo. And from time and time, even with Papa John, the bass player down there, I got on his bass and learned to play the bass a little bit. I learned to play the bass. I still play the bass now, but that's make my fingers look sore. If I play on every night, it wouldn't be sore. But playing once in a while, I get my fingers sore. And I play the South Street on now. Well. My first big band I played was with J. Mike Shane. Oh, yes. The fellow from Kansas City? Yes. Oh, yeah. I heard that band years ago, 1938 or so. Yeah. We used to play down in the world. I used to go from different states with him. Then I played with the James Brothers from Homer. Oh, out west. Yeah. In Louisiana. Yeah. Anybody else in that band from New Orleans that we might know of? Well, with the drummer, he was named Claiborne Williams. Oh. Was it the son of the old man, Claiborne Williams? It was the son. It was the son of him. In other words, they called him Crip. Yeah. Crip. But during the time I learned how to get on to play the piano. Yeah. When did you start on piano? Did you? Well, I started piano in... I started actually on piano in 1928. I actually started on the piano. In fact, I started on the organ. Oh, the little reed organ. Yeah. At school. Yeah. The teachers used to call me up and after recess, I'd be, instead of going on the outside, going in and banging on the organ. By the way, where did you go to school? I went to the Lutheran. I went to J.W. Hoppin. I went to the phone. But you're all here in the... Oh, no. ...in New Orleans. Mm-hmm. And... Did you have any lessons on piano or pick it up or...? No one had never showed me a note on the piano. No, everything I knew, even around guys learning how to read notes. Yeah. I just picked up from experience. My daddy died when I was five. Well, you never did know him so awfully well then. Well, I still remember his face. You remember him well? I remember his face. In other words, my brother's a picture of him. Really? My brother's a picture of my dad. Mm-hmm. But my brother, he couldn't even whistle. He doesn't go into music. He couldn't whistle. He couldn't whistle. Is he older than you or younger? He's older now. He's a year and nine months old now. But my sister could play. My sister, I'm nine years older than my sister, well she started playing after, I started playing the piano. And she used to watch me play the keys. And she took a piano then too? Yeah, she took a piano. Yeah. But so far as me ever learning how to read music, what I learned how to read, I learned to read being all guys. Yeah. Did you have the piano in your home? Never had a piano in my life. Never had a piano in my life. Never had a piano in my life. Never, every time I had a band practice, I would practice at somebody's house, about a few hours a night like that. And I worked with Earl Foster, I worked with him about sixteen years. One man, sixteen years. Just here, I'm working with him, I'm in the county of Zill right now, he's triple right now. But I started off with him when they had four pieces at the Carnival Club on Drive Street, Drive and U-Turk, they had a joint called the Carnival Club. And it was Joe Battley. Joe? Joe Battley, trumpet player. Battley. Battley. Battley, Battley. Battley. Battley. I don't know him. He's a youngster, isn't he? Is he still around? Yeah, he's still around. He's a good trumpet player too. Yeah. In fact, him and I, now that's who actually taught me, him and his boy Cliff Bruce, let me now read a little bit. Joe Battley and Cliff Bruce. Of course, Cliff Bruce, he doesn't play that anymore. You know, like I told you, he passed. You see? But those are the two guys that brought me into music life, into the world. Who was the leader of that band, the Dryads? Earl Foster. Who? Earl Foster. Earl Foster. Oh, yes. Earl Foster, yes. In other words, I played six years straight with him in Buggalos at the Club Plantation. And I worked behind a much more piano player than what I was, but everybody liked my playing better than they did his. He had a good style, I guess, that people liked. He had a better style than he did. Now, in other words, I used to go back to Bazzari's school. Had a boy back that used to teach me, but I don't know, somehow he didn't take up too much time with me, you know then. Yeah. But he had his notes showing me, every boy loves a girl and all that other. Showing me different notes and scales and octaves and how to make it. In other words, he had a whole keyboard on the piano. And he drew a diagram for me to take it home and study. So I did that. So his name was Richard. Richard, that is his last name? No, that's his first name. First name, Richard. That's all I would call him Richard. I never knew his last name. I was going to ask about some of the other piano players when you were even a little kid before you did that. No, the piano players that I really know. When I was a kid, Steve Lewis. Oh, yeah. I never got to hear you. Big Eye Lewis. Big Eye Lewis. There was another guy called... I don't remember. He's still there, but he hasn't played anymore. I don't remember that. One man we never did interview, Walter Deku. I remember Walter Deku too. I was up all. Walter Deku was playing. I went around to Budweiser when Walter Deku was playing. Yeah. I remember when he played. When he played the Budweiser. I was still going. I played with Austin Young. I knew him. I recorded him. Austin Young was playing from all that. I knew him when he played bass. After he lost his teeth, I guess. That's right. He played bass with me. And that's another man that helped me in music work. Helped me in how to run. That's right. We all call him Boots. Yeah. His brother was Sax Sport. That's right. Sport. That's right. Sport. Yeah. I knew him quite well. Good musician. Another was Boots and I were good friends. We just like that. He always called me to my house and showed me some of those different types about music. And how to make it. And change. I knew him. Did you ever know Lester Young? I guess that was his cousin. Yes, he was in California. He was a saxophone player. I met him in Dayton, Ohio. I met him in Dayton, Ohio when I was up there. I first went to Ohio. Can you think of any other piano players now that you remember even before you started playing, when you went to dances or heard them in bands? Well, I always did know Mrs. Kimball. Oh, yes. I knew her before she got married to Mr. Kimball. Yes. And now Miss Dolly, I knew her boys but I didn't know her. Yeah. I knew her boys, the oldest one, not the youngest, the youngest. I only heard her for the first time about three years ago, I guess. Yes. Now, what is this fellow's name? He played piano too. I guess you heard Walter Pijon. Walter Pijon and I, we played a duet just like you did on the day tonight. Oh, yeah. We played a duet at the Opsin House. Now, I remember Fat Pijon when Pijon was playing on the boat, on the steam of the girls there. Yeah. With Faith Marvin there. Well. He was about to remember when they had all that going on at that time. Now, Fat Pijon used to play with Papa Celestine. Many people don't know that, but I know that. I don't remember that. Yeah. He played with Papa Celestine. In other words, he was playing piano with Papa Celestine. Yeah. Not Miss Kim. Fat Pijon was playing. I'm still trying to call this guy his piano player. Stack Lee. Oh, yeah. Stack Lee. Yeah. Stack Lee. Those are the kind of piano players that I came up with. Steve Lewis Stack Lee, Big Eye Lewis, and one more was Toots. His name is Isidore. Isidore Washington is his name. Isidore Washington. But everybody calls him Toots. Toots. Toots. Where did he work? He didn't ever work. Just played around any joint you could have. Any joint he wanted to be around. Yeah. Toots was playing before I got married. I was married in 1932. And Toots was still playing then. Yeah. Did he play house parties and all that? We used to play house parties. Toots would play in one block and I would play the next block. Yeah. House parties. But most people would be at my party. Yeah. You know during that time people would have fish fires and had the red lights on the gate. Yeah. I've heard about that. Well some of them didn't have none. Some of them did have. Some of them would have tickets printed out. Some of them would have notes printed out. You know. But during that time they didn't have none. Different type of police can have that now. Yeah those days are gone I guess as the fish rise and lawn parties. Yeah. Although I used to go to a few lawn parties. During the time I came up. If a man went to jail you had to get up on the steps to get in the patrol. You remember the step patrol? Yeah. Yeah I remember how it was. Well many guys got out the patrol going to jail. Many guys got out jumped out only way going to jail. Yeah. Knocked the fellow off the step and get on the patrol and going about the business. They didn't know who they was no. So in fact I played a birthday party. It was supposed to be a birthday party. Did you have much trouble with the police at those parties? Did they? Yes. In other words during that time they used to sell moonshine liquor during that time. You know. Yeah. They sell that old moonshine liquor. So much of a Coca Cola bottle full of whatever kind of bottle they might put it in. It's settled so much. When the cop knew that you had that liquor going on, he'd come in and get his little graph if he had any given. If he did he'd raid the junk. Yeah. He'd raid the junk during that time. Yeah. But I can remember a gang of things from my teenage years. Now my son, my oldest son now is 33. Where? My son is 33, the oldest son. My youngest son is 26. Which my youngest son is on the police force. Do they play any music? No, he's a piano player. My youngest one. My oldest boy, he's a roofing work. He's a roofing work. He's a roofer. Yeah. That's his occupation. But the youngest one, he took it behind me. I said, show him, you know, sometimes he'd come in from school like that. Well, to keep his mind out, I'd get on the piano, which I bought a piano, you know, since then. Yeah. And bought and put it in my home. So I'd show him a little bit about the piano. Well, since then, he went to school, went to Bush kindergarten. And in fact, I paid for his education, but I didn't get mine. That's why I tell a lot of children today. The children way back is more far off than the children of the day, because the children, they are blessed. Yeah, that's right. That's a lot of opportunity. We had to pay for our learning during that time. If you bought a spell, it cost you a nickel. You get a spell for nothing. A jowler cost me 40 cents when I was going to school. Rift and take cost me 80 cents. Yes, sir. Well, did you always live on this side of the river, I guess, uptown? I always lived in that uptown vicinity. Now, I'm back in the neighborhood where I'm living now. I've been back there 22 years. 22 years. 22 years. 22 years.

Can you remember some of the other bands you've worked with? You told about that first band that you played, the one on Dryad Street. I worked with Paul Barber, I worked with George Lewis, I worked with George Williams, I worked with the average band around here. Yeah, I guess you worked with a whole bunch of them. Yeah, around here. Like most of the musicians. I worked with Kit Howard, Sheik, Thomas, you know I work with Thomas now. I work with Thomas now. But I worked with Peter Burkhardt, I worked with Willie Humphrey, Pryce Humphrey, I worked with all of those guys. I've been playing with all of them since I was a kid. Almost all of them. But they all knew I could play. There's a lot of musicians that say they can play, but they can't play. That's true. Still there's a lot of good musicians here too. Yes. People that I've never heard of. My uncle, you may have known him, Eddie Johnson. Eddie Johnson, the bass player. Oh, the bass player. He was the only bass player besides Tillman and Brown. I knew a few bass players. He plays tuba. He plays tuba. Is he much older than you? My uncle? Oh yes, he's older than my dad. Older than your dad? Yeah. Sometimes, you know, his uncle's just a few years older than a person. Yeah, he's older than my dad. In fact, him and my dad was in the same band. In other words, they used to play for the Jolly Boys and Girls, the Young Men Olympia, and the Mary go around, and the Buzzs and all those people like that. Did you ever play in any brass band, any instrument in the brass band? I never played in a brass band. First day she bought a piano. She bought a piano from the league. She paid ten dollars for the piano. And soon I'd come in from school every evening, I was on the piano. She could call me to watch this show, I was still on the piano. Yeah. Trying to not have to play. I used to take my two fingers and go along the keyboard and listen. Yeah. Other words, I had control of this right hand and never to have control of the left hand. So one day, I heard a guy playing, and I listened to what he was doing on the piano, and from then on I was playing. From playing. Who was it, do you know, that you listened to him? Ian Brose? That was Stackel E. It was Stackel E. Yeah, it was Stackel E. See Stackel E, he said, there were about two doors of me. We lived on Sixth Street then. He's dead now, isn't he? No, he's working back at Millen Home, right now. He is? Where? At Millen Home. He works there? Yes. Back there on St. Bernard. The one down on Franklin and all that? That's right. No, the one on St. Bernard. St. Bernard. Back there on Cadillac Street. Yeah, I don't know of that. Does he still play piano? No, he doesn't play any more. I didn't think so. I mean, I used to hear about him all ten or fifteen years ago a little bit, but then I never, I don't remember if I heard him or not. I might have, on Bourbon Street someplace once, I'm not sure. No. What style did he play? Mostly blues? Well, he was more of a hollong piano player. A what? A hollong piano player, you know. Like the hollong? He was a blues piano, but he was more of a blues man, you know. In other words, he couldn't play too many sentimental numbers. Never could play too many sentimental numbers. But I listened to whatever he did, I tried to learn it myself, but that's what started helping me out, started to learn the keyboard. Now when I first started, I played F sharp. Well, in the black keys. In the black keys. Yeah. A lot of guys I learned to do that. Then, I worked with a group a couple of times, they couldn't even tune up at the piano, and I had a cross chord. In other words, I played E natural, B natural. Yeah. That's the keys I played. And I didn't think I could do it. Well, one mind kept telling me, he said, once you can try to learn the different sounds. So I run the chromatic and then adjust some keys up and down, and see that heavy note in place, you see. Yeah. And that's the main line playing B natural. Many fellows can't play no B natural, E natural, F sharp. They can't play those kind of keys. They can't play D flat. Usually it's a hard key, I can say. Yeah. Somebody can read music, right? Yeah. Bothersome. I was going to ask about some of the different clubs and the old halls, dance halls that you played in, if you can remember. Well, I worked at the Bulls. I worked at the Tulane Club back down on Gravity Street. Yeah, I know. Which bands did you play with then, or did you work by yourself sometimes? No, I never had worked by myself. Up until lately, I do work by myself now. I worked by the gas light on Sunday night by myself. You know, over there. Yeah. But I have worked a gang of jobs by myself. In fact, I worked a job, I didn't want no band, just wanted to play a piano player. And I'm going to play these work jobs myself. Were there any of the other old time dance halls, like, well, the old Economy Hall or Quadraters Hall? Well, I worked at the last round up. I worked at the Lulule. I worked at the Lulule, right down here. Yeah. And this was sent to you down here. I worked at those different clubs. Other way, I worked the last round up. That was the last place closed up down here. That was the last jacket closed up down here, called the last round up. It would be open, the other jacket would be closed. I used to go right down there at night, from seven o'clock at night, and be down there at five, sixty o'clock the next morning. And music was what you call a real deal there. A dollar and a half was plenty money for musicians at that time. A dollar and a half. Depression days, huh? Yes. But I made a dollar and a half. In other words, my tip was more than my salary was. Yeah. My salary was a down and a half. My tip would be about twelve, thirteen o'clock. A night. That wasn't bad then. Yeah. That was every night. But I actually started off playing music out, like I told you, with those guys, Julius Simpson, Eddie Hickman, and Cliff Bruce. Cliff Bruce. I didn't put his name in there, but that's his name, Cliff Bruce. Cliff Bruce. That's his name, Cliff Bruce. And we started there. Yeah. When did you first play with Kid Thomas? After Joe James died. No, he hired Smitty before he got me. But him and Smitty couldn't even get out when I was nice. You had never played with Kid Thomas before in the old days? I had played with Kid Thomas when Kid Thomas was playing across the river at the... What's the name of the place over there? That place is Moulin Rouge. Moulin Rouge. Is that it? Yes. Now, Kid Thomas was playing at Moulin Rouge, and I was working down at Seymour's Coconut Grove. I worked there five years with Earl Foster. In other words, Kid Thomas had his band. He still had the same piano player, and we had four pieces, and Kid Thomas had about six pieces down by the moon. But after we'd knock off, I would go down there sometime, and listen to Kid Thomas play. And sometimes I would sit in with the band. That's during that time. That was around 1940. I'd sit around 46, 46. I remember sitting there on Dad's Dune too. Dad's Dune too. Dad's Dune was a piano player. He used to try to show me how to play piano, but I was much better piano player than him. He was. So instead of him showing me, I used to show him. But he was supposed to be showing me. So he liked it in my style. That's Dune. He was leader of a band then, was he? Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Do you remember who else was in his band at that time? Well, we had a banjo player called Emmet. Emmet. He used to drink too much. I didn't take him away from that drink. I used to tell him all the time, he wouldn't be drinking too much. Did you ever play out at the Millenburg, out the lake there in those camps? I was playing at the Millenburg. I used to play at Mamaloos. Oh, yes. I played at Mamaloos. I used to play at Mamaloos. Yes, I played at Mamaloos. I played at Mamaloos with Kid Clayton. Oh, yes. I knew him. I played out there with Kid Clayton. When he used to go out there and renovate him for fifteen cents. And catch the Smokey Mary train going back there. Plenty of people don't know about the Smokey Mary. I remember the Smokey Mary. Yeah. I remember the Smokey Mary. I used to go back there or catch the Cemetery Court and ride straight on back west end to the end of the line. Where did you play at west end? West end, yes. Did you play at any of the places out there? Camps? That's the Mamaloos. Mamaloos was right on the lake. The camp. That's where I played. Right on the water. I played out there about three years with Kid Clayton. Then I was playing the Badger there. Oh, you played Badger there. I played Badger there. I played Badger there. I played music with Jerry Green, bass player. I played, I come up under Papa John, bass player down there. Slow drag. I don't remember him playing no bass but I remember him being a Grand Martian. I never even knew he could play no bass. I think he was mostly a dancer and he played a little guitar and the homemade bass he finally made himself. Yes. But Punch, you see Punch downstairs, Punch used to coat one of my aintes. I have to make him remember that the name. Punch Miller, he used to coat one of my aintes. Yeah. But he's no relation to your family at first. No, he's no relation to my family at all. He may be related to my daddy, my daddy in the Chamberlain in the Barlet. Yeah. Just like I have an uncle named Eugene Miller. Well, it was a long time before I knew he was my uncle. In other words, I played with Joe Harris, he's a scientist one player too. Yes, I remember he lived up on... Chapitou Street. Chapitou Street. Is he still living there? No, that's my first cousin. Is that right? That's my first cousin to my daddy's people. In other words, Joe Harris was kin to me on my grandfather's side. And I played with him about six years and didn't know it. My first cousin. Didn't know he was my cousin. Yeah, we interviewed him about four or five years ago. Yes. He had some nice pictures of some of the early bands he played in. I don't suppose you have any pictures of any of those early bands that you played in? Oh, no. I had a gang of pictures from Littlewoods. I'm with my second wife now and then my first wife at the road staff. Yeah. So I didn't keep up with too much. Yeah, most people lose those pictures. They don't bother to keep them. Yeah, I didn't keep up with them. They're interesting to look at now. I do have some pictures of Earl Foster at home now. Yeah. With Austin Young and Mr. Willie James and myself. That was the four. That was the band. That was during the time I played at the Coakland Grove across the river. Was Austin playing the trombone there? No, he was playing the bass. Playing the bass. Playing the bass. I took some pictures of him playing bass. I made records of him with some of the bands. It reels almost over, but can you remember anything else about the camps out at the lake and the bands you heard there, what went on out there? Was it mostly private parties or were they clubs open to the public or how? No, these were private parties that we played for out there. Private parties. Yes. These were private parties that we played for out there. When the time I played with Fifth League. Oh. Can you tell us more about the lawn parties? The lawn parties? That you went to and played for and all? Well, most of my lawn parties was at those fraternities up on, uptown. Yeah. Those were the most lawn parties I played. None down here. No. Yeah. And this was sent to down here. And the fish fries when you were a boy? Yeah, fish fries when I was a boy. They had a red light, you say, out there on the street? Red light on the street. On the gate. Yes. Did they charge to get in or did you just go in and buy your fish or what? Just go in and buy your fish. You go in and buy your fish and come out. Some people would stay and listen to the music. Would they have a band or just the piano player usually? The piano player, sometimes a guy would have a guitar and somebody would come out there with a harmonica. Yeah. Red light on the street. We'd start in the evening around at 6 o'clock and round up around 5 o'clock the next morning. Well, they'd go all night then. They'd go all night until the fish was out. That's during my time. Were they mostly right in the house or did they have it out on the lawn? Well, some of them have it in the yard. They'd have tables in all the yard. Yeah. Sit in the yard. You'd be sitting at a table sit in the yard. In other words, during that time people would look for houses with big backyards there to give these poils and fish fries and things. Did anybody just have them or did certain people have them almost every week? Oh, they had fish fries. Some nights they had fish fries two in one block. That often? Just that often. They'd say, well, we go to Miss Elizabeth's house or someone else's house. We go to our fish fries. Or we go to our Miss Phyllis's fish fries. She'd go to the night. They'd always have music though, would they? Oh, they'd always have music. And doing that, if they didn't have music, they had to wind up graffinals, you know, with those big .

12-inch records, big, big records, those large records. The big horn and all, some of them. The horn sticking out on the victuals and all of them. In other words, some of them would stand the victual and wind the victuals, every day they had no piano. Yeah. And a lot of times, guys like I said would come in with the harmonica and guitars and things. They might come in with maybe a G-hop or E-flat harmonica. And if you were any kind of piano player at all, you knew just what he did from the hop that you could tune up. If the piano was in tune. Because most pianos, they don't usually be in tune. Because what the harmonica said, if the harmonica said E-flat and the piano did not tune to 440, you still ought to tune. Different keys. Did they pay the piano players always for the fish fryers? Did you get tips or what did they do? We got chips. A tip from the public. Most pianos, a lot of the time I went on doing that time, I was a drinking man at that time. I'd go home drunk. You know, you wanted to drink I guess too, huh? All I wanted to drink, yeah. We didn't worry about that one. In other words, they'd sell a home brew. They'd sell a home brew and homemade root beer and all that. It's this thing as that. Spiked lemonade up there with rums or something like that. And briney. Spiked it up there. Why did they, did they, in some cities I know they would have a house party to help pay their rent and all that. Did they do that here too? Yes. They did the same thing. A lot of, they gave was for the, for the benefit of raising money for, for churches and sometimes for somebody who was sick and who was disabled. It was usually an idea to raise money, not just, not just only to have a good time but also to raise money. Yeah, to raise money too, yes. Would there be a pretty big crowd there always or sometimes just not much? Well, the crowd would go and come, you know, the crowd would go and come. Sometimes just a few friends would stay all night like that. People would come in all in different hours and get what they want. They would go and come in all in different ways. They would go and come in all in different ways. They would go and come in all in different ways. So the balance of this reel will conclude the interview of James Sing Miller, his interview of December 11th, 1964. Did they have room to dance? Oh yeah, I always had dancing. I always had dancing, I guess. In other words, during that time, see what they used to have, they had, like I said, they had the red lantern on the gate, but they had somebody that would be watching out for the cop too. Yeah. To let you know when the cop was coming. In other words, he knew a sign to give you in case the cop was coming. That means don't play. When it rang when they moved, in other words, they used to have a cowbell, they could pull it, run it a piece of wire. Oh yeah, I've seen those, yeah. Or in the backyard. In the backyard. And when the cowbell rang, you know where the cop was coming, see? Then you'd keep quiet. Then they'd keep quiet. When he come in there, there wasn't nothing to be said. Could they arrest the people sometimes just for making too much noise, the musicians for disturbing the piece? Yes, then you go down the coat, if you go down the coat then, most fines at that time would be about five hours. Yeah, it was a lot of money in those days too. Most, most, yes. That's the biggest fine was on you, about five dollars. Now I've had a fine put on me for one dollar. It was a certain piece, one dollar. Yeah. In that time, wasn't it? Just for playing music, right? Yes, for playing music. Now the coat house was at Tulane and Saratoga at that time. Yeah, I remember that place, I saw that. Yes. Anything else about those fish fries and long parties you can think of? Did they have them all year around or mostly summertime? Well, most summer, summertime. They never gave no fish fries in the wintertime. They didn't have them in the winter? Never had them in the wintertime at all. All summertime. Yeah. I wondered about the parade bands when you were a little kid coming up. Did you ever, before you took up music, did you follow the parades? What were they like in those days? Well, parade bands during that time, when I was a boy, coming up, they most played for the Buzzards and the Lions. Yeah. The Jolly Boys and Girls. They had the Tuxedo Band. Those bands that I remember when I was coming up. Now this Eureka Band is just a new outfit to me. Yeah, that came up later in the 20s, I guess. In the 20s, that's new to me, but the other band that I knew was band during my time. Do you remember Celestine? Was he in the Tuxedo? I remember Celestine when he had a Tuxedo Band. segments.title: Miller's youth, first bands, piano teachers, Earl Foster and New Orleans pianists
segments.summary: Bill Russell opens the 1964 interview. Miller gives his birth and nickname, his piccolo-playing father, learning ukulele, organ and piano by ear, first jobs from 1927, and sixteen years with Earl Foster. He also recalls other New Orleans pianists, house parties and police raids.

segments.title: Bands, clubs, Kid Thomas, Mamaloos camps, fish fries and lawn parties
segments.summary: Miller lists the bands and clubs he worked in, how Stackolee taught him piano, the Last Round-Up, Kid Thomas, Kid Clayton at Mamaloos and the lake camps, and begins describing fish fries and lawn parties.

segments.title: Fish fry rules, parade bands, Chris Kelly, Celestin and a medicine show
segments.summary: Miller finishes on fish fries, police warnings and fines, then recalls parade bands, Chris Kelly's plunger mute, Celestin's band, singers like Bessie Smith, Robichaux, and touring with Earl Foster's medicine show.

segments.title: Medicine show talk, Rena band, second-line bands and jitney dances
segments.summary: Miller discusses whether the medicine was real, the Hadacol show, playing with Kid Rena in 1942, second-line parade bands, and how jitney or tag dances worked.
